Scenes 01 and 02 / What the messages prove

Training scenario · explanation

What the two messages can prove

Neither message proves who is asking. The bank change still needs an independent check.

The email · 16:42

A correct sender address and a familiar conversation do not prove who is writing.

  • A change to bank details always needs an independent check.

The chat · 16:46

A display name and urgency tell you nothing about who controls the account.

  • Anyone can set a name and copy a photo.
  • Pressure to skip a check is a reason to slow down.

Fictional scenario. Guidance: FBI IC3 Business Email Compromise.

Your decision

Discuss before selecting

What should Farid do next?

Your first decision of the day. Vote with a show of hands, then select the answer the room chose.

The invoice is expected. The bank details have changed.
A message using Ravi’s name adds pressure to pay.
Choose an action. What makes your verification route trustworthy?

Verify through a contact you already hold, then follow the normal approval process.

  • Use the supplier record, not the email.
  • Replying to the same email cannot verify anything.

Fictional scenario. Guidance: FBI IC3 Business Email Compromise.

The evidence / Trainer reveal

The callback changes the picture

Farid calls the supplier on the number already held in the finance system.

Re: Invoice MS-1048Evidence recap

Nadia · Maju Supplies <nadia@maju-supplies.example>
Subject
Re: Invoice MS-1048

Hi Farid,

Our bank details have changed. Please use the revised details for today’s payment.

Please complete this before 5 PM. The amount stays the same.

An independent check

Farid calls the number already held in the supplier record.

What information would change your decision?

01
The supplier denies the change

The contact confirms that the existing bank details still apply.

02
Ravi denies sending the chat

Farid checks through the staff directory. IT investigates the account.

03
Farid holds the payment and reports

He preserves the messages and reports them through the approved channel.

Independent verification gives you facts the message never could.

  • Hold the payment, keep the evidence and report.

Fictional outcome. Verification principle: FBI IC3 Business Email Compromise. A matching address does not establish who controls the account.

Documented incident / Hong Kong, January 2024

Real incident · official account

When the meeting looked convincing

A real case: a fabricated video meeting helped convince an employee to transfer about HK$200 million.

HK$200m

Approximate reported loss

A fabricated video conference reinforced an email impersonating a chief financial officer.

01
An email claimed executive authority

The sender invited an employee to a confidential meeting.

02
A prerecorded video supported the story

The official account describes no interaction during the fabricated meeting.

03
Payment instructions continued in messages

The employee authorised transfers to five local bank accounts.

Which independent check could interrupt this sequence?

Even a convincing meeting can be fabricated.

  • A separate, authorised payment check is what stops the loss.

Source: Hong Kong Government LCQ9, 26 June 2024. Text reconstruction from the official account. No original victim messages or video shown.

Module 1: The borrowed identity

Why this matters

Anyone can copy a name, photo and job title, and messages that borrow a familiar identity get trusted.

Who you will meet

AinaOperations
SitiCommunications

Module 1 / The borrowed identity

Course definitions

Impersonation and phishing

Three words we use all day.

Impersonation

Claiming a trusted identity

A person, colleague, supplier or service that you already know.

Phishing

Persuading you to take a harmful action

Pay, sign in, share information, approve access or open something.

Spear phishing

Targeting a particular person or group

The message is shaped around your role, project or contacts.

Identity on a screen is easy to borrow.

  • Verify the person through a route you already trust.

Course paraphrases of the terms. Taxonomy and guidance: FTC Business Impersonator Scams; MITRE ATT&CK T1566.

Scene 03 / Aina’s public profile

Training scenario · fictional profile

What can someone learn about Aina?

Everything on Aina’s public profile that a stranger could reuse.

Aina
Operations Coordinator at Meranti1
Public profile · Fictional social network
Aina · 3 days agoExcited to start the Riverside office move2 next month! Thanks Farid and Ravi3 for the support, and our partners at Maju Supplies4.
Aina · 1 week agoLooking forward to the regional operations forum on Thursday5. See you there!

Discuss in pairs: what could a stranger reuse?

  1. 1Job title. Lets a message mention her real work.
  2. 2Project. Makes “about the Riverside move…” sound expected.
  3. 3Colleague names. A sender can name-drop to seem connected.
  4. 4Supplier name. Invoices or requests can borrow it.
  5. 5Event date. Tells a stranger when she is away from her desk.

Public work details make a fake message feel expected.

  • Knowing them does not prove the sender works with you.

Scene 06 / Brand impersonation · fictional brand

Training scenario

The support page that found you

Aina complains publicly about a login problem and “support” replies within minutes.

social.example / Aina’s post

An unsolicited support contact

It offers to fix an account issue. Who started this conversation?

The reply asks for a code: never send one. Its address is not the one Aina has saved.

If support found you, do not use it.

Not every advert or reply is malicious. The route you choose is what keeps you safe.

Response / Cloned profile or takeover

Training scenario

Someone is using your name

What to do when someone pretends to be you, and how that differs from someone taking over your account.

The situation · fictional

Colleagues tell Aina that “Aina” is messaging them for documents. She did not send these messages.

01
Preserve the profile details.

Profile link, handle, screenshots and times.

02
Report and warn affected contacts through a trusted channel.

Tell security or communications for work-related impersonation.

03
Use official account recovery if the genuine account is compromised.

Then review sessions and connected apps with support.

Fictional scenario. Guidance: FTC Business Impersonator Scams.

Response / Cloned profile or takeover · continued

Training scenario

Copied profile or taken-over account?

Which action fits which situation.

ActionCopied profileTaken-over account
Preserve link, handle, screenshots and times✓✓
Report the copy to the platform✓—
Use official account recovery; review sessions and apps—✓
Warn contacts through a trusted channel✓✓

A copied profile needs a platform report; a taken-over account needs official recovery.

  • Both need you to warn contacts through a trusted channel.
  • Password changes alone do not remove a copied profile.

Fictional scenario. Guidance: FTC Business Impersonator Scams.

Module 2 / The trusted request · Scene 08

Training scenario · Thursday

An urgent request from the manager

“Ravi” asks Farid to pay a new supplier now and approve it later.

RaviWorkplace chat · display name and photo shown

Sure. Should I raise it through procurement first?Farid · 14:21

The deadline is close

The normal approval process still applies.

Scene 08 / What changed

Training scenario

What the pressure asks you to skip

The three pressure tactics hidden in one short message.

RaviThe final message, enlarged
Handle this before the 3 PM meeting.1 Keep it between us for now2 — I’ll approve it later.3Ravi · 14:22

Three pressure tactics · anyone can feel them

  1. 1Urgency. “Before the 3 PM meeting” leaves little time to check.
  2. 2Secrecy. “Keep it between us” stops others from noticing.
  3. 3An exception to normal approval. “I’ll approve it later” removes the control that protects the payment.

Urgency and authority are reasons to check, not reasons to skip the check.

  • Each tactic tries to remove a check. The risk is the exception, even if the sender is genuine.

Fictional scenario. Guidance: FBI IC3 Business Email Compromise.

“I can help once I confirm through our normal approval process.”

2

Card 2 · Senior colleague

Training scenario

The voice on the phone

A caller knows Aina’s name and manager, and asks her to read out a code.

Incoming call · “IT service desk”Read aloud by the trainer · photo is an illustration
CallerHi Aina, this is Jason from the IT service desk. Ravi asked us to look at your account.

Scene 09 / A phone call · continued

Training scenario

What proves who is calling?

What to do when a caller asks for a reset or a code.

Remember

Knowing names does not prove identity.

  • Hang up.
  • Call the service desk using its known number.
  • Never read out a sign-in code.

A caller can learn your name, your manager and your projects from public details. A genuine service desk can wait while you call it back.

Fictional script. Helpdesk and voice impersonation guidance: Joint Scattered Spider advisory, 29 July 2025 update.

Synthetic media / Course guidance

Course guidance

A face or voice cannot approve a payment

Why spotting a fake video is not a reliable defence.

Fictional: a video call that looks and sounds like Ravi asks Farid to release an urgent payment. Documented: in the Hong Kong case, the meeting was a prerecorded video with no interaction.

Spotting glitches

Odd lip movement, blurred edges, a flat voice

Limit Realistic media may show none of these, and a recording needs no live reaction. Useful to notice, unreliable as the only defence.

Independent verification

Call back on a known number; use the authorised payment workflow

Works either way It does not depend on judging the media. A genuine Ravi can approve through the same process.

A separate, authorised payment process works whether the video is real or fake.

  • Do not rely on spotting glitches.
  • Not every video call is unsafe, and not every fake is detectable.

Sources: Hong Kong Government LCQ9, 26 June 2024; FBI IC3 Business Email Compromise.

Module 2

Module 2 takeaways

  1. Urgency, secrecy and “approve it later” are pressure tactics.
  2. A face, a voice or a caller’s inside knowledge does not prove identity.
  3. Genuine requests still follow the approval process.

Your habit from this module

Call back on a number you already have before you pay, reset or share.

Module 3 / The message that fits your job

Training scenario · three inbox messages

A message that fits your work

Three ordinary work messages, each asking for a different risky action.

Calendar · Ravi’s assistant · 08:55

Riverside move: updated agenda — Accept the invitation and sign in to view the agenda.

Requested action: sign in with a work account from a link.

HR Benefits · 09:10

Confirm your 2027 benefits by Friday — Update your bank and ID details to keep your cover.

Requested action: disclose personal and bank information.

Document shared with you · 09:31

Q4 supplier review — Farid shared a file with you. Open to review and comment.

Requested action: open a document, possibly followed by a sign-in.

Three questions for every message

1
Who is asking?
2
What would I authorise or disclose?
3
How can I verify outside this message?

Look for the action, then verify outside the message.

  • Sign in, share data, open a file: each is a request.
  • Any of these messages could be genuine.

Fictional messages. Phishing channels and targeted lures: MITRE ATT&CK T1566; Microsoft evolving identity attacks, 29 May 2025.

Scene 11 / Read the destination

The destination behind the label

Who really controls this link? Vote, then see how to read it.

Email · link label

Please review the agenda on the Meranti document portal before the meeting.

Link preview (not opened)

https://login.company.example.attacker.test/review

attacker.testThe domain at the end of the hostname controls the site.login.company.exampleWords on the left can be any text the owner chooses./reviewThe path, after the first single slash, is not the owner.

Inert text using reserved .example and .test names. Nothing here navigates.

Preview without opening

Vote: which organisation controls this address?

Read the hostname from the right, up to the first single slash.

Answer

The last part, attacker.test, owns the site.

  • Read the web address from the right, up to the first single slash.
  • A familiar-looking link can also be abused through redirects or genuine hosting, so the request still needs checking.

Fictional scenario. Guidance: MITRE ATT&CK T1566.

Scene 15 / Shared files

Training scenario · no file opens

A shared file is still a request

Shared files and attachments that lead to a sign-in or download.

Document shared with you · Maju Supplies

Nadia shared “Q4 statement” with you. Open to review. You may be asked to sign in.

PDF

Q4-statement.pdf

Can carry a link to a sign-in page.

HTML

Invoice-viewer.html

Can show a sign-in form once opened.

SVG image

Signed-contract.svg

An image that can contain links or scripts.

These formats are everyday examples, not automatic signs of an attack.

A shared file is still a request

Did Aina expect this file? What happens after she opens it?

A file type or brand does not make it safe.

  • If you did not expect it, check with the sender through a known contact first.
  • Open the known storage app, or ask Nadia through the established contact, before an unexpected sign-in or download.

Fictional files. Attachment and file-sharing lures: Microsoft Email threat landscape Q1 2026, 30 April 2026; Microsoft evolving identity attacks, 29 May 2025.

Table exercise · show of hands

Would you approve this?

Four realistic requests: decide for each whether to proceed, verify first, or hold and report.

Proceed, verify first, or hold and report? Tables vote with a show of hands for each card, then reveal.

Card 1 · Finance

Nadia (known supplier contact): “Our bank has changed. New details on our letterhead attached.”

Verify first Genuine change, not yet approved: call the established contact, then complete approval.

Card 2 · Operations

Siti’s usual chat account: “Can you add me to the payroll folder? IT is slow today.”

Verify first Genuine account, someone else using it: check with Siti through the directory and report.

Card 3 · Everyone

Notice inside the IT portal Aina opened herself: “Laptop update on Saturday. No action needed.”

Proceed Genuine notice found through a known route; it asks for nothing sensitive.

Card 4 · Finance

“Ravi”: “Skip the second approval on this transfer. I’m boarding a flight.”

Hold and report Not Ravi: an impersonated urgent exception. Verify through the directory.

Some requests are genuine.

  • The right answer depends on the action and the route, not on calling everything phishing.

Fictional cards. Guidance: FBI IC3 Business Email Compromise; NIST SP 800-50 Rev. 1, September 2024.

Signals that do not prove safety

Training reference

The signals that do not prove safety

Six common “safety signs” and what each one really proves.

SignalWhat it establishesWhat it does not establish
Familiar logo

Someone used that image.

Logos are easy to copy.

Known sender

The message came from, or claims, that address.

Accounts can be compromised; display names can be faked.

HTTPS padlock

Your connection to that site is encrypted.

Who runs the site, or why it asks.

No email warning

Filters did not flag it.

Filters miss new and targeted messages.

Fluent wording

Someone wrote it carefully, possibly with AI help.

Grammar is a weak signal of intent.

MFA completed

Someone passed a sign-in check.

That the business request is valid.

None of these signals validates the request.

  • HTTPS still matters: it protects the connection, not the request.

Fictional scenario. Guidance: Microsoft evolving identity attacks, 29 May 2025; Microsoft AI-enabled device-code campaign, 6 April 2026.

Route 2

The staff directory, the supplier record, or a number you already hold.

Module 4

Module 4: Beyond the password

Why this matters

Attackers no longer need your password if you approve a sign-in, a code, an app or a device for them.

Who you will meet

AinaOperations
MeiIT support

By the end you will be able to

  • Explain what an approval actually grants
  • Respond to sign-in prompts you did not start
  • Recognise code, app-permission and device-linking tricks

Module 4

Words we will use

Six words for this module, in plain language.

You do not need the technical detail.

For each one, ask what it gives, and to whom.

MFA
A second check when you sign in, such as an app prompt or a code
Session
Staying signed in after you log in, so you are not asked again
Device code
A short code that signs another device in to your account
App permission
Letting an app read or change your mail and files
Linked device
Another phone or computer that can use your account
Phishing-resistant MFA
Security keys or passkeys that only work on the real site

Module 4 / Beyond the password

Course explanation

Access can be granted without sharing a password

Four ways to give someone access without sharing a password.

Login session

You signed in this morning. The browser keeps you signed in.

Grants: whoever holds that session can act as you until it ends.

MFA request

“Approve sign-in to your Meranti account?”

Grants: access for the sign-in attempt that triggered it, wherever it came from.

App permission

“Meeting Helper wants to read your mail and files.”

Grants: the app can use that data, often without asking again.

Linked device

“Link a new device to your messaging account.”

Grants: that device can read and send messages as you.

A session, an MFA approval, an app permission or a linked device can each let someone act as you.

  • None of them needs your password to be shared.
  • Check what access you are granting: what does it give? To whom? Did you start it?

Course explanation. Sources: Microsoft evolving identity attacks, 29 May 2025; Microsoft AI-enabled device-code campaign, 6 April 2026.

Sign in from your bookmark or app, not from a link.

  • Phishing-resistant MFA (security keys and passkeys) blocks this relay, and MFA still blocks many attacks, so keep using it.
  • Report any sign-in page you reached from a message.

Documented incident / July 2022

Real incident · first-party disclosure

A defence that stopped the attempted access

A real case where staff entered passwords but security keys stopped the attack.

3

Employees entered credentials

Cloudflare reported three credential submissions on a phishing page. Hardware-key requirements prevented the attempted access.

01
Text messages targeted employees

They pointed to a lookalike sign-in page (July 2022).

02
Three people submitted credentials

The page captured what they typed.

03
Security keys stopped the sign-in

The keys only work with the genuine site, so the attempted access did not succeed.

Strong controls and quick reporting work together.

  • Some MFA types resist phishing much better than others.
  • Keys do not stop consent or payment fraud, so the other checks still matter.

Source: Cloudflare phishing incident disclosure, 9 August 2022; CISA phishing-resistant MFA fact sheet, October 2022. Course summary of the company’s own account.

Documented technique / February 2026

Concept reconstruction

A browser problem becomes a repair request

A documented technique: a fake extension breaks your browser, then offers a harmful “fix”.

CrashFix

A browser problem becomes a repair request

Microsoft described a fake browser extension that caused problems, then offered a harmful “fix”.

Install software and get fixes only through approved sources and your IT team.

01
Installation

A browser extension posing as a familiar ad blocker is installed.

02
Delay

Nothing seems wrong at first, so the problem is not linked to the install.

03
Problem

The browser starts crashing or stops working.

04
Repair pretext

A message offers a fix that asks the person to run something themselves.

Source: Microsoft CrashFix, 5 February 2026. Concept reconstruction, not the actual extension, messages or code.

Module 6 / Stop the chain · tabletop · continued

New exercise · fresh facts

How the tabletop runs

Four evidence cards, one at a time. Record four things for each.

For each evidence card, record

  1. Known facts
  2. Unverified claims
  3. Next safe actions, each with an owner
  4. A short report

How it runs

Roles first, then four evidence cards one at a time, then a short debrief.

Do not decide that one event caused another without evidence. Write hypotheses separately.

You do not need the full picture to report.

  • Report what you saw and let the right team connect the dots.

Module 7 / Report and recover

Our course mnemonic · not an official framework

Pause, verify, report, recover

Four steps to remember for any suspicious request.

Pause

Pause the sensitive action.

For example: hold the payment; do not approve the prompt yet.

Verify

Verify through an established route.

For example: call the supplier from the record, or the colleague from the directory.

Report

Report uncertainty or a mistaken action.

For example: “I entered a code at 14:05 and I’m not sure the page was ours.”

Recover

Follow recovery instructions.

For example: sign out where IT asks, and let the responsible team decide next steps.

Ask the room for one example of each from their own work.

Sources: NIST SP 800-50 Rev. 1, September 2024.

After a mistake

Course synthesis

What happened determines the response

What to do depends on what happened.

Clicked

Stop interacting. Report exactly what you did.

Security checks whether anything downloaded or ran.

Entered credentials or approved access

Report immediately through a trusted route.

IT / security revoke sessions and app grants, then reset as needed.

Ran software or allowed control

Stop. Contact IT from another device if needed.

IT / security contain the device. Avoid an unplanned wipe or restart.

Transferred money

Tell finance and security. Contact the bank now.

Finance uses the bank’s established fraud channel and keeps records.

Reporting a mistake quickly is the right thing to do, and it is never blamed.

  • A password reset alone may not remove access. Report early so the right team can check sessions, apps and devices.
  • The coloured label on each card shows who follows up. Your job is to report quickly and honestly.

Course synthesis, not verbatim official instructions. Sources: FBI IC3 Business Email Compromise; Microsoft AI-enabled device-code campaign, 6 April 2026.

  2. Module 2Call back on a number you already have before you pay, reset or share.

  4. Module 4Approve only what you started and recognise.
  5. Module 5No ticket you raised, no remote access.
  6. Module 6Report early, even if you are not sure.
  7. Module 7Pause, verify, report, recover.
